raw_case_text:
A 58-year-old woman was admitted in our clinic with a history of recurrent necrotizing lymphadenopathy. In the personal history she disclosed that she was treated for hypothyroidism and she had an episode (2006) of vesiculobullous dermatitis which was diagnosed as contact eczema. She gave a negative history for any travel abroad and prior contact with pet.
She complained onset of painful left axillary lymph node package associated with fever (38 C) in February 2008. For that problem she was followed in the oncology department from 2008 to 2010. At the beginning of 2008 the first biopsy with histology suggestive but not diagnostic for Castelman's disease was made. For persistent symptoms a full-body CT scan was performed with detection of left axillary and supraclavicular lymph node package (8 x 6 cm with colliquative area), reactive lymph nodes (2 cm) in the right axilla (2 cm), inguinal lymph nodes (2 cm), nodules of uncertain origin (<1 cm) in the lung, and liver parenchyma. Repeated lymph node biopsy was not yet conclusive for diagnosis of Castleman's disease.
For persistent fever inguinal biopsies were performed in June 2009 and February 2010 with confirmation of nonspecific necrotizing lymphadenitis. Microbiology and virology analysis were negative (in particular, HHV-6 and HHV-8). The full body CT scan of June 2010 showed right axillary and supraclavicular lymph nodes (up to 2.8 cm), no finding of colliquated lymph nodes previously described on the left, enlargement of inguinal lymphadenopathy bilaterally, right perianal mass (1.3 x 1.1 cm) similar to abscess, no more evidence of liver and lung lesions. On a CT scan performed for a sudden extremely painful nose swelling, a mucous obliteration of the maxillary sinus was revealed, nose soft tissues were thickened and swollen without osteostructural alterations (Figure 1). At the revision of previous histological biopsy samples, disclosure of necrotizing lymphadenitis with epithelioid/giant cells and vasculitis in the absence of lymphoproliferation signs was observed. These aspects were considered as not inconsistent with vasculitic disease. A first rheumatologic evaluation was carried out in January 2011. Physical examination revealed swelling with features of chondritis and crusted lesions in the nose and the right ear (Figures 2 and 3); chronic conjunctivitis with blepharitis aspects (Figure 4); multiple purple skin areas suggestive for vasculitic lesions in the upper and lower limbs, in particular ulcerative injuries of the hands (palm) (Figure 5) and ulcerative rhagadiform lesion in the gluteal region were disclosured as well as papular-crusted eruptions in the abdominal and umbilical area. Evening fever was persistent and relapsing. Palpable axillary and inguinal lymph nodes were painless, elastic, mobile; the remainder of thoracic and abdominal examination was unremarkable. In the suspicion of granulomatous vasculitis, nasal mucosa biopsy was performed. Histologic findings did not show specific aspects for Wegener's diagnosis: acute and chronic infiltrate was revealed but no evidence of vasculitis, necrosis or plurinucleate cells. Laboratory studies proved neutrophilic leukocytosis and elevated acute-phase reactants. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) were negative but anti-Beta 2 glycoprotein 1 autoantibodies IgG and IgM and anti-Cardiolipin autoantibodies IgG and IgM gave positive results. Among microbiology and virology analysis performed, IgM Cytomegalovirus-antibodies (with negative antigenemia) and IgM Epstein-Barr virus antibodies (with not significant PCR amplification) were found. Bartonella serology was also tested with disclosure of anti-Bartonella henselae levels corresponding to 1 : 128.
At the second rheumatologic evaluation the positivity of anti-Beta 2 glycoprotein 1 autoantibodies and anti-Cardiolipin autoantibodies was confirmed as well as anti-Bartonella levels (1 : 128). Considering persistent fever and skin lesions, in spite of steroid therapy previously adminisetred (prednisone 37.5 mg/day), infectivologic examination was required. Although Bartonella serology was considered aspecific finding as part of a more probable vasculitic disease, it was decided to administer antibiotic therapy in the suspicious of Bartonella lymphadenitis (Azitromicina 500 mg for 5 days). After the antimicrobial therapy (June 2011) lymphadenopathies, fever and vasculitic skin lesions gradually resolved. Given that vasculitic origin was still assumed, the patient was assigned to the rheumatologic followup to study the possible evolution of the disease. However, a persistent resolution of the previous clinical picture was observed at the evaluation of February 2012.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 58-year-old woman presented in January 2011 with a 3-year history of relapsing evening fevers and recurrent necrotizing axillary, supraclavicular, and inguinal lymphadenopathy, accompanied by painful nasal and right ear chondritis, chronic blepharoconjunctivitis, and ulcerative/vasculitic skin lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Beginning in February 2008, the patient developed a painful left axillary lymph node mass and fever (38 °C), followed by relapsing evening fevers, bilateral axillary, supraclavicular, and inguinal necrotizing lymphadenitis (repeatedly biopsied in 2008, June 2009, and February 2010), transient subcentimeter lung and liver nodules, a right perianal abscess-like mass, and acute painful nasal swelling with maxillary sinus obliteration despite oral prednisone (37.5 mg/day). At rheumatologic evaluation in January 2011, she exhibited nasal and right auricular chondritis, chronic conjunctivitis/blepharitis, and ulcerative purpuric/vasculitic skin lesions on the palms, gluteal region, and abdomen.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypothyroidism on hormone replacement and a prior episode of contact vesiculobullous dermatitis (2006). Social history: no foreign travel and no reported pet contact.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for relapsing evening fevers (38 °C), recurrent lymphadenopathy, painful nasal and right ear swelling/crusting, chronic conjunctivitis/blepharitis, and palmar, gluteal, and abdominal ulcerative/vasculitic skin lesions. Medication: oral prednisone 37.5 mg/day.

objective.physical_examination: January 2011 exam: relapsing evening fever; swelling, chondritis, and crusted lesions of the nose and right ear; chronic conjunctivitis with blepharitis; multiple purple vasculitic skin lesions on upper and lower limbs including palmar hand ulcers, a gluteal ulcerative rhagadiform lesion, and papular-crusted abdominal/umbilical eruptions; painless, elastic, mobile axillary and inguinal lymph nodes; unremarkable thoracic and abdominal exam.
objective.routine_investigations: Neutrophilic leukocytosis and elevated acute-phase reactants; ANCA negative; positive anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I IgG and IgM and anti-cardiolipin IgG and IgM autoantibodies (confirmed on repeat testing); positive CMV IgM with negative CMV antigenemia; positive EBV IgM with non-significant EBV PCR amplification; negative HHV-6 and HHV-8; and positive anti-Bartonella henselae antibody titer at 1:128 (confirmed on repeat testing).
objective.advanced_workup: 2008 full-body CT showed an 8 x 6 cm left axillary/supraclavicular colliquative lymph node package, 2 cm right axillary and inguinal nodes, and <1 cm lung and liver nodules; June 2010 full-body CT showed right axillary/supraclavicular nodes (up to 2.8 cm), bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy, a 1.3 x 1.1 cm right perianal mass, and resolution of left axillary, lung, and liver lesions; sinus CT showed maxillary sinus mucous obliteration and nasal soft-tissue swelling without bone destruction. Re-review of 2008-2010 lymph node biopsies revealed necrotizing lymphadenitis with epithelioid/giant cells and vasculitis without lymphoproliferation; nasal mucosal biopsy showed non-specific acute and chronic inflammation without granulomatous vasculitis or necrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with chronic relapsing necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis with cutaneous/cartilaginous vasculitis and secondary antiphospholipid antibody positivity associated with Bartonella henselae infection (confirmed by persistently positive anti-Bartonella henselae titer 1:128 and complete clinical resolution following targeted antibiotic therapy; Castleman's disease, Wegener's granulomatosis, and active CMV/EBV/HHV-6/HHV-8 viral replication ruled out, with positive CMV/EBV IgM representing cross-reactive/non-specific serology alongside negative CMV antigenemia and EBV PCR). After steroid therapy (prednisone 37.5 mg/day) failed to control relapses, administration of oral azithromycin (500 mg daily for 5 days in June 2011) led to complete and sustained resolution of lymphadenopathy, fever, and vasculitic skin lesions through February 2012 follow-up.
